opening.headline: Find out which services are affected when you receive an end-of-life announcement and learn how to create a transition plan complete with evaluation gates and phased deployment.
body: One day, a notice arrives from the model provider that a particular model will soon be shut down. The notice only has the model name, end date, and recommended replacement model and does not list our services. However, the model name is written here and there in the configuration file as well as in the code and prompt templates, and after the end date, requests to call that model will fail.

In this class, we will first compare the items that the three companies' end-of-support documents contain in common, and check what the model ID and alias are fixed and what is moving. Next, we look at API transitions and platform name changes that occur separately from model replacement, and why prompts are not directly transferred between models. At the end, we walk through the thought process of determining the transition order in a situation where 50 services are using one model.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the structure of end-of-support documents and migration guides for models and APIs
Determine if your transition plan includes evaluation gates and phased deployment
Describe how evaluation sets, passing criteria, and canary deployments reduce the risk of model replacement

screens.title: A product discontinuation notice has arrived, but who is affected?
screens.lead: Select each service box below to see where each service uses its model name. Some are hidden outside of configuration files.

visual.alt: An image showing a discontinuation notice email with several service boxes underneath it, with a question mark indicating which box is affected.
labels: Model name hidden in prompt template

items.prompt: Notice: There is only model name and end date
items.answer: The notice only states which model will be terminated and when and what it is recommended to move to. The notice does not tell us where in our organization that model is used. Finding your sphere of influence is up to you from the start.

items.prompt: Code: Model strings are hardcoded all over the place
items.answer: If you write the model name for each service directly in the code, the same string will be scattered in dozens of places. If even one part is missed when switching, only that service will stop on the end date.

items.prompt: Hiding: In prompt templates and batch jobs
items.answer: Configuration files can be found by searching, but it's easy to miss model names written in prompt templates or monthly batch jobs. Paths that are rarely called on a regular basis are only revealed as failures shortly after the end date.

items.prompt: Result: If the end date passes, the call fails.
items.answer: Anthropic informs you that requests sent to a retired model will fail, and OpenAI also explains that the model or endpoint can no longer be accessed at the point of termination. Any call party that is not found in advance will be an obstacle on the end date.

screens.outro: Now that we know what the problem looks like, let's think about a similar experience.

screens.title: Think back: The last time you changed models
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: There has been a discontinuation notice, but I don't know which services are affected. Have you ever seen a similar situation?
items.answer: First-time users read the notice and immediately start searching for codes. However, code search shows only a portion of what is being called. This lesson ensures that usage records are the most accurate, where they are actually called.

items.prompt: Have you ever been surprised by the change in output format or tone after changing the model?
items.answer: It's common for the same prompt to vary in length, format, and tone when added to a new model. This is why it is dangerous to think that just changing the model name completes the transition. A transition is not about changing names, but rather seeing a change in behavior.

items.prompt: Have you ever counted how many places the model name is written in the code?
items.answer: If you've never counted them, it means you can't predict your switching costs. If the names are gathered in one place, it's easier to control the order of transitions; if they're spread out, all services have the same risk on the same day.

screens.outro: We will now compare how the three companies structure the end of support.

screens.title: Common structure of three company termination documents
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google guide notice periods, status terms, and fallback models.

visual.alt: Schematic showing the lifeline and notification period intervals of model states from active to terminated.
labels: End date, after which request failed

tabs.label: common elements
tabs.body: All three company documents provide a table of end dates for each model and recommended replacement models. Notices are posted both in email and in documents, and the documents have terms to indicate status. So when you read a new notice, you always want to check the same four things: current status, end date, recommended replacement model, and notice period.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI has a minimum notice period unless there are other issues. The general public model will last at least 6 months, specialized variants of the general public model will last at least 3 months, and preview models with preview in their name can last much shorter, such as 2 weeks. Deprecated is a state in which the termination process has begun and an end date has been set, while legacy is a state in which it is no longer renewed and may be terminated in the future. The end date can also be monitored programmatically by checking the `shutdown_date` field of the model as `GET /v1/models`.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body: Anthropic describes model life in four states: Active, Legacy, Deprecated, and Retired. Deprecated still works, but is not recommended, and has a fallback model and end date. Retired causes the request to fail. For publicly released models, we provide at least 60 days notice prior to termination. Dates in the document apply to Anthropic-operated routes; Amazon Bedrock and Google-managed Google Cloud-provided routes have their own shutdown schedules, so dates may vary even for the same model.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body: The end of support table for the Gemini API has a shutdown date and recommended replacement column. Some models will say 'No shutdown date announced' (no shutdown date announced), while others will indicate that the endpoint will be automatically routed to the new model without being shut down. End-of-support announcements are posted in the release notes, and the earliest announced end date is maintained in this table. A blank end date does not mean permanent support.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the status terminology, let's see what the model ID and alias pin it to.

screens.title: Model IDs and Aliases: What's Fixed and What's Moving
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare whether our calls move or stop when the new model comes out.

visual.alt: Schematic comparison of how a fixed snapshot continues to point to one model, while an alias moves to a new snapshot.

states.label: Fixed snapshot ID
states.body: Starting with generation Claude 4.6, undated IDs (e.g. `claude-sonnet-4-6`) are not aliases, but rather fixed snapshots themselves. Anthropic does not change the weight or composition of existing model IDs, but releases improved versions with new IDs. So even if a new model comes out, our call stops and we use the same model, and if we want to change it, we have to change the ID. Each ID also has a separate retirement and termination schedule. It is also important to note that the notation is different for each cloud. Bedrock prefixes it with `anthropic.`, and Google Cloud's previous generation IDs prefix the date with `@`.

states.label: alias
states.body: 4.6 Previous generation models have snapshots with date IDs (e.g. `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`), and undated names (`claude-sonnet-4-5`) are aliases that point to the most recently dated snapshot of the same minor version. Although aliases are convenient, there is a risk that what they point to may change, resulting in a difference between the evaluated model and the operating model. This is the same principle behind version pinning in software dependencies. The build tool's dependency locking document also explains that if you leave the version flexible, a successful build yesterday may fail when released with a different version today, and locking ensures that the same input is always released with the same version, providing reproducibility. The results can be predicted when the model call is also evaluated and the ID is used as is in the operation. Also keep in mind that even with the same ID, the observed behavior may differ slightly if the serving infrastructure changes. The Gemini documentation also shows an example of endpoints being automatically routed to a new model when it is released.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at API transitions and name changes that occur separately from model replacement.

ext.title: Gradle User Manual: Locking dependency versions

screens.title: Responses API conversion and platform name change
screens.lead: Below is a summary comparing the inputs and outputs of the old and new methods. Select the underlined passages to see how the structure changes.

data.text:
Chat Completions: Input and output are Message array and Receives multiple creation results with n parameters.  
Responses: Input and output are Item unit (message, function_call, etc.), and only one generated result is returned. Tool calls can be repeated multiple times within a single request, as specified by Agent loop is the default.  
Google Platform: Service name is Changed from Vertex AI to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.  
Gemini API: Available within the same library as Differentiate between Developer API and Gemini platform through client settings.

marks.note: Chat Completions send and receive messages with multiple interests attached to one object. Responses divide them into independent units called Items.

marks.span: Receives multiple creation results with n parameters
marks.note: Code that relies on this parameter will not work as is when moved to Responses. Responses removes this parameter and returns only one result at a time.
Message is also a type of Item, and function_call and function_call_output are also Items. The code that parses the response should be changed to read the output array rather than the choices array.
A model can call a web search, file search, code interpreter, remote MCP, or user function multiple times within a single request. The number of calls, latency, and cost assumptions change.

marks.span: Changed from Vertex AI to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
marks.note: Changing the service name is a transition that requires creating a correspondence table separately from replacing the model to match the document, console, and permission names. For example, Vertex AI Studio became Agent Studio on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

marks.span: Differentiate between Developer API and Gemini platform through client settings
marks.note: The google-genai library differentiates between the two services by client settings such as enterprise, project, and location, so you can switch without having to rewrite your entire code.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified a transition that changes structure, let's see if the same prompt behaves the same in other models.

screens.title: Prompt portability: Does the same statement work the same in different models?
screens.lead: Read the table to compare how the same request differs between the old and new models. You can see why switching just by changing the model name can be risky.

screens.outro: Now, let's apply it to a case and explain the procedure for finding the scope of influence.

screens.title: Eval and Canary Deployment: How to determine if a model can be changed
screens.lead: Below is a hypothetical example showing evaluation and incremental deployment in one file. The intent is to demonstrate the concept, not the actual product setup format. Select a line range from the description on the right to see what each block does.

data.code:
service: contract-summary
baseline_model: "model-a       " #Model currently in operation
candidate_model: "model-b      " #model you want to change
eval_set:
  size: "200                   " #Representative number of inputs picked from actual requests
  include: [General Agreement, Very Long Agreement, Blank Inputs, Ambiguous Clauses Document]
criteria:
  - name: "format_valid        " #Is the output in JSON format as promised?
    method: code_check
    min_pass_rate: 0.99
  - name: "key_terms_covered   " #Have you missed any key provisions?
    method: rubric_grader
    min_pass_rate: 0.90
  - name: length_within_limit
    method: code_check
    min_pass_rate: 0.95
gate: all_criteria_pass_and_not_worse_than_baseline
rollout:
  traffic_steps_percent: [1, 10, 50, 100]
  hold_each_step: 1d
  rollback_if: format_valid_below_0.99
  keep_previous_model_route: true

notes.note: The starting point for comparison is to place the model you are currently using (baseline) and the model you want to change (candidate) together in the same service. If you only look at the results of the new model, you cannot tell if it has improved, and you must compare it with the previous model with the same input to see any changes.

The evaluation set consists of representative inputs that resemble the distribution of real requests and edge cases such as long inputs, empty inputs, and ambiguous inputs. Since the model may have different expressions even with the same input, it is judged based on the passing rate for each criterion for a representative set of inputs rather than checking whether the output string is exactly the same like a unit test.

Standards are determined by what is important in the service. Criteria that can be checked in code, like formal compliance, are quick and reliable, but they don't see subtle qualities. Criteria such as whether or not key content is included are scored by humans or models using a rubric (grading table), but the reliability of this scoring method itself must first be confirmed and expanded. The passing threshold is determined according to the risk level of the service, and the numbers here are assumed values.

Gates are conditions for going to the next step. It only passes if all criteria cross a threshold and it is no worse than the previous model. If you pass on just one criterion because it looks good, you miss out on the decline caused by the other criteria.

A canary deployment involves applying a change to only a subset of traffic, evaluating the results, and then increasing the rate. The goal is to limit and revert affected users when something goes wrong. You need to write down the revert conditions in advance and leave a path to the previous model to actually revert.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the principles of evaluation and gradual deployment, let's move on to an example and explain the order of finding the scope of influence first.

ext.title: Anthropic: Define success criteria and build evaluations
Google SRE Workbook, Chapter 16: Canarying Releases

screens.title: Commentary 1: Find the scope of influence first
screens.lead: 50 services use one model, and the end date is set. Select the arrows to the right to follow the instructor's steps in finding your sphere of influence.

steps.title: Move notice to table
steps.body: Create the first row of the table by pulling the model, end date, and recommended replacement model from the announcement. For example, if the notice specifies an end date and a replacement model, the base date in the table is the end date. This table is the starting point for all subsequent steps.

steps.title: Find actual call destination with usage history
steps.body: Export usage in the console to get usage details by API key and model to see where calls are actually being made. Anthropic provides instructions on how to click Export on the Console's Usage page to receive a CSV for each key and model. There is no need to rush to find places that are not called even if they have names in the code, and you must first find places that are called even if they are not visible in the code.

steps.title: Contrast with Code Search
steps.body: Retrieves the model string from the code repository and matches it against the list of callers. Calls that are present in Usage but not in Code Search are a sign that they are hiding in prompt templates, external settings, or other repositories. Conversely, if something is present in the code but not in usage, it may be dead code.

steps.title: Classify services
steps.body: Categorize services by traffic, mission criticality, and prompt dependency. Services with small traffic, low importance, and simple prompts are candidates for moving first, while services that are sensitive to output formats are candidates for stricter evaluation criteria.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: No transition schedule will be finalized until this table is completed. A schedule made without knowing the scope of influence is destroyed by one hidden call point.

screens.outro: Now that we have found our sphere of influence, let's decide in what order we will move it next.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Transition sequence and evaluation gate
screens.lead: This time, we build a transition roadmap based on the sphere of influence table. Select the right arrow to see the gate conditions for each step.

steps.title: From low-risk services
steps.body: Start with low-risk, low-traffic services and move to the new model to measure the impact of the change. Once you see what surprises the first service brings in request format, response structure, and cost, you'll have a checklist for the remaining 49.

steps.title: Setting evaluation standards for each service
steps.body: Each service sets an evaluation standard that collects representative inputs and compares the output of the old model and the new model. Determine items that are important to the service, such as format compliance, length, and factual accuracy. Anthropic also advises testing replacement models well in advance of their end date to gauge their performance.

steps.title: Progressive deployment of only passing services
steps.body: Only services that pass the evaluation will direct some of their traffic to the new model and gradually increase the rate. The path to revert to the previous model is left until the end date. An irreversible transition leaves you with no options when something goes wrong.

steps.title: Schedule backwards from the end date
steps.body: Count backwards from the end date and schedule all services to be completed well before the end date. Since the notice period is 6 months for OpenAI's public model and 60 days for Anthropic's, it is safer to plan manpower based on the shorter notice period.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: A plan without evaluation gates and phased deployments is a replacement gamble, not a conversion. Impact studies, evaluation gates, incremental deployment, and a return path must all be present before it can be called a transition plan.

screens.outro: In the final commentary, we'll look at how to change the structure to make the next transition less painful.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Changing to a structure that does not rely on aliases
screens.lead: Switch between the current structure and the improved structure to compare where changes need to be made when replacing the model.

states.label: Now: model names are scattered
states.body: Model strings are scattered throughout service code, prompt templates, and batch scripts. To replace a model, you need to change the code of each of the 50 services, and you can only find out which service has been changed to the new model by opening the code. If you are using an alias, it is difficult to notice if the object you are referring to changes. Since we have no control over the order of transitions, all services have the same risk on the same day.

states.label: Improved: Reference by role name in one configuration
states.body: Model IDs are collected in one place, and services are referred to by role names, such as 'for summary' or 'for classification'. When replacing a model, there is only one setting to change, and the order of transfer for each service can also be controlled by setting. Prompt templates leave model-dependent assumptions as evaluation criteria rather than comments. That way, you can run the same evaluation in a new model and immediately see if the assumption is broken. Using a fixed snapshot ID prevents the evaluated model from changing from the operating model.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the entire transition flow, let's summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key Takeaways: Transition Planning Requirements
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard.

paragraphs: The discontinuation notice is a table with end dates and replacement models. Notice periods and status terms vary from company to company, but the order in which notices are read is the same. Check the current status, end date, recommended replacement model, and notice period.

The model ID can be either a static snapshot or an alias that points to the latest. Since generation 4.6, Claude's undated ID is a static snapshot. Also remember that each ID has its own termination schedule.

Transitions that change API or service names should be planned separately from model replacement. The Responses API has a different input/output structure, and changing the platform name changes the name of the document and console. Prompts and parameters may not transfer directly between models.
The transition plan must include impact studies, assessment gates, phased deployment, and a return path. If any of these four things are missing, it's not a plan, it's just a schedule.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The transition doesn't end with just changing the model name. Move only services that have passed the evaluation in stages, leaving a way to revert.

screens.outro: Lastly, we will check the requirements that the plan must meet in a table.

screens.title: Transition Planning Checklist
screens.lead: Each row of the table is a requirement that your transition plan must have. Read about what problems they prevent and what happens when they are missing.

data.notes: The content of each requirement varies depending on whether the conversion is a model replacement, API structure change, or service name change. Check any type of conversion against these five requirements.

glossary.def: The shutdown process for the model or endpoint has begun. An end date and recommended replacement model will also be established.
It will no longer be renewed, but its termination has not yet been confirmed. It's a sign that it could end in the future.
The ID points to a specific snapshot, and the alias is a name that follows the most recent snapshot.
This is an OpenAI API that handles input and output on an item basis and provides a tool call loop as standard.
This is the extent to which the same prompt operates with the same quality even if the model is changed.

The evaluation set is a set of inputs that represent actual requests and is used to measure pass rate against service-specific criteria. Canary deployment is a method of sending only a portion of traffic to a new model to check the results and increase the ratio.

misconceptions.myth: A model ID without a date always leads to the latest model.
misconceptions.fact: After generation 4.6, Claude's undated ID is a static snapshot. Aliases that follow the latest snapshot are the way they were in models prior to 4.6.

misconceptions.myth: Just change the model name to complete the conversion.
misconceptions.fact: Parameters, response structures, and incident settings may vary together. For example, in Sonnet 5.5, thinking disabled may result in a 400 error and the response may begin with a thinking block.

misconceptions.myth: It is enough to find out when the notice comes.
misconceptions.fact: Compare your usage history with your code searches so you can quickly determine the scope of your impact. The notice period varies depending on the company and model, from a minimum of 2 weeks to 6 months.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The notice includes an end date and recommended replacement model, and notice periods vary by company.
Model IDs are fixed snapshots or aliases, and termination schedules are separate for each ID.
API conversion and platform name changes are planned separately from model replacement.
Evaluation gates, phased deployments, and return paths are at the core of any transition plan.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: How many places does the model name appear in our code and prompt templates, and if the end date is set today, where should we start looking?

checks.q: Which of the following is correct about IDs without dates on Claude models after the 4.6 generation?
options: It is not an alias, but a fixed snapshot itself, so the object it points to does not change automatically.
The nickname always refers to the latest snapshot, so it automatically changes when a new model is released.
The notation is the same in Bedrock and Google Cloud, so the ID can be copied as is.
If the ID is the same, the observed behavior is completely the same even if the serving infrastructure changes.
checks.explain: Undated IDs from generation 4.6 onwards are static snapshots. In previous models, names without dates were nicknames for the latest ones.

wrong.1: This is the description corresponding to the undated name of the previous model.
wrong.2: Bedrock is anthropic. The prefix, Google Cloud, is written differently by using @ before the date.
wrong.3: If the serving infrastructure, such as a router or classifier, changes, the behavior may change slightly.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. The results will not be recorded, so feel free to choose.

checks.q: After replacing the model, the code that read content[0].text of the response was broken. What is the most likely cause?
options: The dateless ID became an alias and called another model.
Changed to Responses API, message array disappeared
The response may start with a thinking block, so the first element is not body text.
The text was truncated because the incident token was charged as an output token.
checks.explain: When adaptive thinking is turned on by default, responses can start with a thinking block, breaking code that assumes the first element is the body.

wrong.0: A fixed snapshot ID does not change the model it points to.
wrong.1: API conversion is a separate issue and this symptom comes from the response block order.
wrong.3: Charging is a matter of cost and has nothing to do with the order of response arrangement.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. The results will not be recorded, so feel free to choose.

checks.q: What is the appropriate reason why it is difficult to judge model replacement based solely on whether the output string for the same input is the same as before?
options: This is because new models always give longer answers than previous models.
This is because expressions can vary even with the same input, so they must be compared based on passing rates for each standard such as format compliance or accuracy.
This is because one input is enough for the evaluation set.
This is because Canary deployment completely replaces evaluation.
checks.explain: Model output may have different expressions, so it is difficult to judge its quality through matching tests. Service-specific standards are applied to representative input bundles to compare pass rates, and even after they pass, the scope of influence is limited to canaries.

wrong.0: Length is just one of the criteria for evaluating each service and is not always longer.
wrong.2: One case does not represent the distribution or borderline cases.
wrong.3: Canaries are a device to limit the scope of influence and are not a substitute for prior assessment.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. The results will not be recorded, so feel free to choose.
